text:
An all-women panel is **not, by itself, evidence of bias against you**. It’s reasonable to want reassurance that the process was fair, but neither the panel’s composition nor the successful candidate’s sex establishes discrimination.

The announcement also isn’t enough to compare your qualifications fairly. Your credentials and experience sound relevant, but her international project leadership may have matched important selection criteria. A short announcement won’t capture her full record or either candidate’s interview performance.

I would focus first on **how the decision was made**, rather than the panel members’ sex:

- Follow up on your request for written reasons. Ask for the selection criteria, their weighting, your assessment or scores, and an explanation of the decisive differences, insofar as disclosure is permitted.
- Check the recruitment policy and applicable public-service rules. Some jurisdictions require gender-balanced panels; if that applies, an all-women panel could raise a procedural issue, though it would not automatically establish discrimination.
- Look for concrete irregularities: sex-related remarks, criteria changed during the process, inconsistent treatment, conflicts of interest, or an explanation that doesn’t match the advertised requirements.

Two weeks without a reply does not itself indicate wrongdoing, but **check any complaint or appeal deadlines now**—waiting for reasons may not stop the clock.

So: don’t frame the panel’s composition as an accusation on the facts available. Do check whether it complied with the rules and pursue a clear explanation of the selection.

Which country or jurisdiction is the ministry in? That will determine the relevant panel rules, disclosure obligations and deadlines.
